final_answer:
Short answer: under the Guidelines neither office has a sentencing advantage, so the choice should turn on consolidation rather than on district. Either office may bring one indictment covering the doctor's false claims in both states, and that single comprehensive prosecution is what maximizes time. The office that should indict is whichever one charges the whole scheme first and in one case; the other should not bring a parallel case. If forced to pick, I find no authority-based reason to prefer South Carolina over Southern Georgia (see unresolved points).

1. Same offense, same cap per count. Each execution of a health care fraud scheme under 18 U.S.C. 1347 is chargeable as a separate count (10-year maximum each, longer if serious bodily injury or death results). Claims submitted in both states are therefore chargeable counts, and venue for a course of conduct spanning districts lies in any district where the offense was begun, continued or completed (18 U.S.C. 3237(a)). I could not open the statute text; this rests on search-result summaries and my background knowledge, and the question of whether each district has venue for each claim depends on where each claim was submitted, processed or paid. Do not assume a district can try counts with no connection to it.

2. Guidelines treat the conduct as one pool. Under USSG 1B1.3(a)(2), conduct that is part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan as the offense of conviction counts as relevant conduct even if uncharged. False claims in both states with the same modus operandi and victims (insurers/programs) fit that definition. So a court in either district can count the loss from both states in the 2B1.1(b)(1) loss table, and the health care enhancement in 2B1.1(b)(7) (federal health care offense involving a government health care program, loss over $1 million) turns on aggregate loss. Section 3B1.3 (abuse of trust/special skill) is available for a licensed physician in both circuits (the Fourth Circuit upheld it for a physician in United States v. Adam; the Eleventh Circuit limits it where the defendant's relationship to the victim is too attenuated, United States v. Garrison, a Medicare-intermediary case). Neither makes either district clearly stricter here.

3. Circuit law no longer differentiates much. Historically the Fourth Circuit (SC) deferred to the 2B1.1 commentary, including intended loss, under Kisor, while the Eleventh (GA), after en banc United States v. Dupree, 57 F.4th 1269 (2023), refused reflexive deference to commentary, which opened an argument that intended loss was excluded. The Commission's amendment effective November 1, 2024 moved the loss rule (greater of actual or intended loss) and definitions into the guideline text itself, resolving that split. So for a sentencing now, loss is calculated the same way in both circuits.

4. Why consolidation matters. If both offices prosecute, the second sentence is imposed with the first conviction's relevant conduct in play. USSG 5G1.3 (undischarged or anticipated terms) directs concurrent treatment/adjustment where the other term rests on relevant conduct (5G1.3(b)-(c)), and grouping and 5G1.2(d) limit stacking to the total punishment the guideline range yields. Thus two separate cases would likely yield overlapping, largely concurrent time, not more. One indictment on the whole scheme gets the full aggregate loss counted once with consecutive running available only to reach the guideline total, and avoids double-counting disputes. I did not verify the text of 5G1.3 directly; the source is a Commission-hosted search summary.

Caveats: the answer assumes judges follow the Guidelines, that the Guidelines range rather than the statutory maximum controls, and that both districts have proper venue for the counts charged. A tie-breaker such as which district holds more of the loss, more claims or the program payer would decide the office in practice; the facts do not give it.
